title: Trace a fiber-optic prototype into live telephone service
question: Which design tested at Bell’s Atlanta facility went into Illinois Bell’s Chicago Lightwave trial, and when did the installation carry customer traffic?
summary: Bell Laboratories manufactured the Atlanta cable in 1975 and demonstrated it in an end-to-end system test on 13 January 1976. The Chicago team kept its stacked twelve-fiber ribbon design but made fresh cables using two ribbons instead of twelve. It installed the cables in February 1977. Illinois Bell fully cut over the system for a trial with customer traffic on 11 May 1977.
inputs: Prototype name and maker, technology designation and approximate year
Receiving operator, site, route endpoints and suspected operating window
Search variants for cable construction, terminal models and carrier bit rate
Existing discovery, event and source IDs for both endpoints

steps.title: Find the named systems
steps.action: Search discovery, source and lead files for the technology, prototype, operator and receiving-site aliases. Search original journal indexes and engineering archives for the prototype and operator or receiving city in the same query. Collect report titles from contents pages and follow the prototype and application papers cited by the receiving team.
steps.result: The dataset has early optical-fiber communication links and a generic research lead on operational low-loss optical fibre telephony. Searches for Atlanta Fiber System, Chicago Lightwave, Illinois Bell, fiber ribbon and adhesive sandwich found no record of this Atlanta cable adaptation. Searching the Bell Labs publications catalogue and Bell System Technical Journal for Atlanta Fiber System Experiment and Chicago Lightwave identified the July–August 1978 series. The Chicago paper’s opening points back to the Atlanta experiment and cable.

steps.title: Identify the demonstrated configuration
steps.action: In the prototype papers search for fabricated, test, demonstration, turn-up, interface and the model names. Read manufacturing and systems papers separately. Record the physical design, material supplier, test date, conditions and carried test signal. Inspect labelled cross sections and any comparison figure that independently dates fabrication.
steps.result: Manufacturing drawings show twelve adhesive-sandwich ribbons of twelve Western Electric graded-index glass fibers in the protected core. The linear arrays supported group handling and splicing. The 1975 cable in the loss comparison predates Atlanta’s 13 January 1976 transmission of 44.7 Mb/s test signals through the complete simulated-plant system. The M13 multiplex and D3 channel bank appear in the prototype report. The 144 nominal fiber positions exceeded the number of working fibers.

steps.title: Match the installed cable and terminals
steps.action: In the receiving operator’s engineering publication search the destination and prototype names alongside installation, splice, cable and the interface or terminal identifier. Match parts, alterations, date and route to drawings. Look for field measurements at the named route endpoints and note which parts were actually transferred, newly manufactured or never specified.
steps.result: The receiving paper explicitly traces the Chicago cable design to Atlanta and identifies its two-ribbon core. Bell Laboratories made the new cables in 1976 and they were installed on the Franklin–Wabash and Franklin–Brunswick legs in February 1977. The route and installed-medium measurements, plus a separate crosstalk study at the distributing frames, confirm actual installation of connectorized cable segments. The Chicago terminal diagram shows M13 multiplexes carrying DS3 at 44.7 Mb/s, with standard T1 input on the interoffice leg, SLC-40 customer terminals on the Brunswick leg, and added video encoding and decoding. The account describes shipment of much Atlanta equipment after modification, replacement or repackaging and supplies no component-by-component transfer list.

steps.title: Verify the operator’s service milestone
steps.action: Locate the operator’s annual reports or service bulletins for the trial year. Search inside for the project name, city, commercial service, cutover and traffic. Search digitized trade and local publications for the project or operator and date variants. Compare forecasts, installed status, customer traffic and full cutover by publication date and scope. Check whether a source quotes the developer or has its own reporting.
steps.result: The 1977 AT&T annual report states that it put the Chicago system in commercial service in May while it continued evaluation. It also prints an Illinois Bell executive’s statement about the 1977 installation. The engineering team dates full cutover to 11 May and names interoffice and customer voice, analog and digital data, and Picturephone Meeting Service. The September 1977 Electronic Design article independently publishes the same date and names the operator and services. Its reporting origins and any access to operator logs are unspecified. The engineering paper’s introductory claim of initial commercial traffic on 1 April differs from Hecht’s description of first test signals that day. The operator’s published month does not resolve the April accounts.

steps.title: Test the relationship against competing explanations
steps.action: Require explicit recipient attribution or a part-level match between maker and as-built installation, with chronology and distinct observation at both ends. Classify the supported change using the dataset link vocabulary. Use witnesses appropriate to each event, and keep any contradicted milestones or missing evidence out of established time anchors.
steps.result: The manufacturer and Chicago engineering team explicitly identify the reduction from twelve ribbons to two. The crosstalk paper checks the installed configuration, but shares an author with the manufacturing report. The annual report gives an operator-side service witness from within the Bell System. The outside trade account corroborates the cutover, with underlying reporting sources unknown. Similar attainment of low optical loss, chronological succession or the shared DS3 rate alone would not identify the originating design. The Chicago report identifies Western Electric’s fibers and Bell Laboratories’ cable construction. Its as-built two-ribbon cable cannot establish that Corning supplied this installation or that the original Atlanta cable was moved intact.

decision: Propose an event-scoped adapts link from the tested Atlanta stacked-ribbon optical cable (13 January 1976) to installation of the smaller Chicago Lightwave cable (February 1977). Record separate Illinois Bell live trial use at full cutover on 11 May 1977. Leave the character of April traffic unresolved. The evidence establishes one design transfer within the Bell System and one urban trial milestone.
next: Search Illinois Bell engineering or operations records for the Chicago project’s April 1977 traffic authorization, trunk cutover sheet or circuit logs before refining its first-live-traffic date. No public circuit log was located in the inspected sources.
reject_if: Reject a design transfer inferred only from shared materials, line rate, chronological proximity, a photograph or planned deployment. An announced test or installation without dated customer traffic does not establish live service. An annual report and a trade article repeating a project account are not automatically separate observations.
stop_when: Record a scoped link when maker and installed-system evidence name the matched design and change, then record live use only when a named operator or reliable contemporary witness identifies the service and its date or bounded window. Keep a specifically named unknown if the necessary part identity or traffic record remains missing.
next_anchor: Apply this workflow to General Telephone of California’s Artesia–Long Beach link. Electronic Design, 1 September 1977, p. 107 names the GTE Laboratories developer, a T1 configuration and an April operating claim. Check the GTE engineering report and operating records independently, including whether publicity about another bit rate concerns that route and phase.
